¶
'''waywise''' (wā′wīz), ''a.'' [< ''way''<sup>1</sup> + ''wise''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''way-witty''; see also ''waywiser''.] Expert in finding or keeping the way; knowing the way or route. ''Ash.''

'''waywiser†''' (wā′wī″zėr), ''n.'' [= D. ''wegwijzer'', a guide, = G. ''wegweiser'', a way-mark, guide, = Sw. ''vägvisare'' = Dan. ''vejviser'', a guide, a directory; as ''way''<sup>1</sup> + *''wiser'', shower, indicator, < ''wise''<sup>3</sup>, point out, show, + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] An instrument for measuring the distance which a wheel rolls over a road; an odometer or perambulator.
{{smaller block|I went to see Colonel Blount, who showed me the application of the ''way-wiser'' to a coach, exactly measuring the miles, and showing them by an index as we went on. It had three circles, one pointing to the number of rods, another to the miles, by 10 to 1000, with all the subdivisions of quarters. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Aug. 6, 1657.}}}}

'''way-witty†''', ''a.'' [ME. ''weiwitti''; < ''way''<sup>1</sup> + ''witty''. Cf. ''waywise''.] Same as ''waywise''.

'''waywode, waywodeship.''' Same as ''voivode, voivodeship''.

'''wayworn''' (wā′wōrn), ''a.'' Wearied or worn by or in traveling.
{{smaller block|A ''way-worn'' traveller. {{right|''Longfellow'', Hyperion, iii. 2.}}}}

'''waywort''' (wā′wėrt), ''n.'' The pimpernel, ''Anagallis arvensis''. [Prov. Eng.]

'''wayz-goose†''', ''n.'' [An erroneous spelling of *''wase-goose'', < ''wase''<sup>1</sup> + ''goose''.] '''1.''' A stubble-goose; hence, a fat goose—that is, one ready to kill in harvest-time.—'''2.''' An entertainment

readings.c3s1:
¶
{{smaller block|<poem>My ancient incantations are too ''weak.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., v. 3. 27.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>How vain is Reason, Eloquence how ''weak!''
If Pope must tell what Harcourt cannot speak.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', On the Hon. S. Harcourt.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>One equal temper of heroic hearts,
Made ''weak'' by time and fate, but strong in will
To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Ulysses.}}}}

(''f'') Incapable of support; not to be sustained or maintained; unsupported by truth, reason, or justice: as, a ''weak'' claim, assertion, argument, etc.

{{smaller block|A case so ''weak'' and feeble hath been much persisted in.
{{right|''Hooker.''}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>I know not what to say; my title ’s ''weak''—
Tell me, may not a king adopt an heir?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., i. 1. 134.}}}}

(''g'') Deficient in force of utterance or sound; having little volume, loudness, or sonorousness; low; feeble; small.

{{smaller block|A voice, not softe, ''weake'', piping, womannishe.
{{right|''Ascham'', The Scholemaster, p. 39.}}}}

(''h'') Not abundantly or sufficiently impregnated with the essential, required, or usual ingredients, or with stimulating or nourishing substances or properties; not of the usual strength: as, ''weak'' tea; ''weak'' broth; a ''weak'' infusion; ''weak'' punch.

{{smaller block|<poem>Sip this ''weak'' wine
From the thin green glass flask.</poem>
{{right|''Browning'', Englishman in Italy.}}}}

(''i'') Deficient in pith, pregnancy, or point; lacking in vigor of expression: as, a ''weak'' sentence; a ''weak'' style.

{{smaller block|<poem>There are to whom my satire seems too bold: . . .
The lines are ''weak'', another ’s pleased to say.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Imit. of Hor., II. i. 5.}}}}

(''j'') Resulting from or indicating lack of judgment, discernment, or firmness; arising from want of moral courage, of self-denial, or of determination; injudicious: as, a ''weak'' compliance; a ''weak'' surrender.
readings.c3s3:
{{smaller block|<poem>Ac grace groweth nat til goode wil gynne reyne,
And ''wokie'' thorwe good werkes wikkede hertes.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xv. 25.}}}}

¶
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become weak. ''Chaucer.''

'''weak-built''' (wēk′bilt), ''a.'' Ill-founded. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Yet ever to obtain his will resolving,
Though ''weak-built'' hopes persuade him to abstaining.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 130.}}}}

'''weaken''' (wē′kn), ''v.'' [< ''weak'' + ''-en''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To become weak or weaker: as, he ''weakens'' from day to day.
{{smaller block|<poem>Somewhat to ''woken'' [var. ''wayken''] gan the peyne
By lengthe of pleynte. ''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 1144.</poem>
<poem>His notion ''weakens'', his discernings
Are lethargied. ''Shak.'', Lear, i. 4. 248.</poem>}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To make weak or weaker; lessen or reduce the strength, power, ability, influence, or quality of: as, to ''weaken'' the body or the mind; to ''weaken'' a solution or infusion by dilution; to ''weaken'' the force of an argument.
{{smaller block|So strong a Corrosive is Grief of Mind, when it meets with a Body ''weakened'' before with Sickness.
{{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 60.}}
In all these things hath the Kingdome bin of late sore ''weak’nd.'' ''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., ii.
<poem>A languor came
Upon him, gentle sickness, gradually
''Weakening'' the man, till he could do no more.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Enoch Arden.}}}}

'''weakener''' (wēk′nėr), ''n.'' One who or that which weakens.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|wayward|6857|weakener}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|the person is full of self-will, which asserts itself against those whose wishes ought to be deferred to or whose commands should be obeyed. ''Contrary'' and ''untoward'' express the same idea, the one in a positive, the other in a negative form. ''Contrary'' is an energetic word, expressing the idea that one takes, or is disposed to take, the course exactly opposite to that which he is expected or desired to take. Contrariness, when ingrained, becomes perverseness: as, a ''contrary'' disposition; a ''contrary'' fellow. This use of ''contrary'' is by many considered colloquial, but has the recommendation of figurative force. ''Contrary'' and ''untoward'' view the person as one to be managed; ''untoward'' views the person also as the object of mental or moral discipline: this perhaps through its use in Acts ii. 40. An ''untoward'' person is not responsive to persuasion, advice, influence, or requests; ''untoward'' circumstances are similarly such as do not help us in our plans. All these words imply that the only consistency in the person’s conduct is in this self-willed independence of others’ wishes or opposition to them, but ''untoward'' implies it least. See ''perverse''.}}

'''way-warden''' (wā′wâr″dn), ''n.'' A keeper or surveyor of roads.
{{smaller block|''Woodcutter.'' Had’st best repent and mend thy ways.
''Peasant.'' The ''way-warden'' may do that; I wear out no ways; I go across country.
{{right|''Kingsley'', Saint’s Tragedy, ii. 6.}}}}

'''waywardly''' (wā′wä̤rd-li), ''adv.'' In a wayward manner; frowardly; perversely.

'''waywardness''' (wā′wä̤rd-nes), ''n.''   [< ME. ''weiwardnesse'', perverseness; < ''wayward'' + ''-ness''.]   The character of being wayward; frowardness; perverseness.
{{smaller block|The unruly ''waywardness'' that infirm and choleric years bring with them. {{right|''Shak.'', Lear, i. 1. 302.}}}}

'''waywise''' (wā′wīz), ''a.''   [< ''way''<sup>1</sup> + ''wise''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''way-witty''; see also ''waywiser''.]   Expert in finding or keeping the way; knowing the way or route.   ''Ash.''

'''waywiser†''' (wā′wī″zėr), ''n.''   [= D. ''wegwijzer'', a guide, = G. ''wegweiser'', a way-mark, guide, = Sw. ''vägvisare'' = Dan. ''vejviser'', a guide, a directory; as ''way''<sup>1</sup> + *''wiser'', shower, indicator, < ''wise''<sup>3</sup>, point out, show, + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   An instrument for measuring the distance which a wheel rolls over a road; an odometer or perambulator.
{{smaller block|I went to see Colonel Blount, who showed me the application of the ''way-wiser'' to a coach, exactly measuring the miles, and showing them by an index as we went on. It had three circles, one pointing to the number of rods, another to the miles, by 10 to 1000, with all the subdivisions of quarters. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Aug. 6, 1657.}}}}

'''way-witty†''', ''a.''   [ME. ''weiwitti''; < ''way''<sup>1</sup> + ''witty''. Cf. ''waywise''.]   Same as ''waywise''.

'''waywode, waywodeship.''' Same as ''voivode, voivodeship''.

'''wayworn''' (wā′wōrn), ''a.'' Wearied or worn by or in traveling.
{{smaller block|A ''way-worn'' traveller. {{right|''Longfellow'', Hyperion, iii. 2.}}}}

'''waywort''' (wā′wėrt), ''n.'' The pimpernel, ''Anagallis arvensis''. [Prov. Eng.]

'''wayz-goose†''', ''n.''   [An erroneous spelling of *''wase-goose'', < ''wase''<sup>1</sup> + ''goose''.]   '''1.''' A stubble-goose; hence, a fat goose—that is, one ready to kill in harvest-time.—'''2.''' An entertainment given by an apprentice to his fellow-workmen, of which the goose was the crowning dish; hence, in recent times, a printers’ annual dinner, the funds for which are collected by stewards regularly appointed by “the chapel.”

'''we''' (wē), ''pron.''; pl. of ''I''<sup>2</sup>.   [Early mod. E. also ''wee''; < ME. ''we'', < AS. ''wē'' = OS. ''wī'' = OFries. ''wī'' = D. ''wij'' = OHG. MHG. G. ''wir'' = Icel. ''vēr'', ''vær'' = Sw. Dan. ''vi'' = Goth. ''weis'', < Teut. *''wīz'', *''wīs'', with appar. nom. suffix ''-s'', prob. = Skt. ''vayam'', we. The L. and Gr. forms are different; L. ''nos'', pl. (including dual), = Gr. νώ, dual; Gr. ἡμεῖς, we, appar. belonging to the stem of ἐμέ, etc., me (see ''me''<sup>1</sup>). In AS. ''wē'' had a dual, ''wit'', which disappeared in the earliest ME. period. See ''I''<sup>2</sup>, ''me''<sup>1</sup>, ''our'', and ''us''.]   I and another or others; I and he or she, or I and they: a personal pronoun, taking the possessive ''our'' or ''ours'' (see ''our''<sup>1</sup>) and the objective (dative or accusative) ''us''.
{{smaller block|Go ''we'' now on goddes halue.
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2803.}}}}
{{smaller block|How goes the day with ''us''? O, tell me, Hubert.
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, v. 3. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|On the left hand left ''wee'' two little Islands.
{{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 8.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>It may be that the gulfs will wash ''us'' down;
It may be ''we'' shall touch the Happy Isles,
And see the great Achilles, whom ''we'' knew.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Ulysses.}}}}
{{smaller block|''We'' is sometimes, like ''they'', vaguely used for society, people in general, the world, etc.; but when the speaker or writer uses ''we'' he identifies himself more or less directly with the statement; when he uses ''they'' he implies no such identification. Both pronouns thus used may be translated by the French ''on'' and the German ''man'': as, ''we'' (or ''they'')}} say, French ''on dit'', German ''man sagt''.
{{smaller block|<poem>Yet seen too oft, familiar with her [vice’s] face,
''We'' first endure, then pity, then embrace.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Essay on Man, ii. 220.}}}}
{{smaller block|The instances in which ''our'' feelings bias ''us'' in spite of ourselves are of hourly recurrence.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Social Statics, p. 196.}}}}

{{smaller block|Many tongues have a double first person plural, one inclusive and one exclusive of the person or persons addressed: one ''we'' which means ‘I and my party,’ as opposed to you; and one that means ‘my party and yours,’ as opposed to all third persons.
{{right|''Whitney'', Life and Growth of Lang., p. 219.}}}}

{{smaller block|''We'' is frequently used by individuals, as editors and authors, when alluding to themselves, in order to avoid the appearance of egotism which it is assumed would result from the frequent use of the pronoun I. The plural style is used also by kings and other potentates, and is said to have been first used in his edicts by King John of England; according to others, by Richard I. The French and German sovereigns followed the example about the beginning of the thirteenth century.}}
<poem>''We'' charge you, on allegiance to ''ourself'',
To hold your slaughtering hands.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., iii. 1. 86.}}}}

{{smaller block|''We'' and ''us'' are sometimes misused for each other.}}
<poem>To poor ''we''
Thine enmity ’s most capital.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., v. 3. 103.}}}}

{{smaller block|Nay, no compliment: . . . Shall ’''s'' to dinner, gentlemen?
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, ii. 2.}}}}

{{smaller block|Our bodies themselves, are they simply ours, or are they ''us?''
{{right|''W. James'', Prin. of Psychol., I. 291.}}}}

'''We-uns''' (literally, we ones), we or us. [Dialectal, southern U. S.]

{{smaller block|“Grind some fur ''we-uns'' ter-morrer?” asked Ab. “I’ll grind yer bones, ef ye’ll send ’em down,” said Amos.
{{right|''M. N. Murfree'', Prophet of the Great Smoky Mountains, ix.}}}}

'''weabit,''' ''n.'' See ''way-bit.''

'''weak''' (wēk), ''a.''   [< ME. ''weik, weyk, waik, wayk,'' a northern form (< Icel. ''veikr, veykr'') taking the place of the southern form ''woke, woc, wake, wac,'' < AS. ''wac, waac,'' pliant, weak, easily bent, = OS. ''wēk'' = D. ''week'' = MLG. ''wēk,'' LG. ''week'' = OHG. ''weih,'' MHG. G. ''weich'' = Icel. ''veikr, veykr,'' rarely ''vākr'' = Sw. ''vek'' = Dan. ''veg,'' pliant, weak; from the verb appearing in AS. ''wīcan'' (pret. ''wāc,'' pp. ''wicen'') = OS. ''wīkan'' = OFries. ''wīka, wiaka'' = D. ''wijken'' = OHG. ''wīkkan,'' MHG. ''wīcken,'' G. ''weichen,'' give way, yield, = Icel. ''vīkja'' (pret. ''veyk,'' pp. ''vikinn'') = Sw. ''vika'' = Dan. ''vige,'' turn, turn aside, veer; cf. Gr. εἴκειν (for Ϝείκειν), yield, give way, = L. √ ''vic'' in ''vītare'' (for *''vicitare''), shun, avoid, *''vix, vicis,'' change. To the same root are referred ''wick''<sup>1</sup>, ''wicker''.]   '''1.''' Bending under pressure, weight, or force; pliant or pliable; yielding; lacking stiffness or firmness: as, the ''weak'' stem of a plant.
{{smaller block|<poem>For men have marble, women waxen, minds,
And therefore are they form’d as marble will;
The ''weak'' oppress’d [impressed], the impression of strange kinds
Is form’d in them by force, by fraud, or skill.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 1242.}}}}
'''2.''' Lacking strength; not strong. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') Breaking down under force or stress; liable to fall, fail, or collapse under strain; incapable of long resistance or endurance; frail, fragile, or resistless: as, a ''weak'' vessel, bridge, rope, etc.; a ''weak'' fortress.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>How ''weak'' the barrier of mere Nature proves,
Oppos’d against the pleasures Nature loves!</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Tirocinium, l. 169.}}}}
<poem>The gate,
Half-parted from a ''weak'' and scolding hinge.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', The Brook.}}}}

(''b'') Deficient in bodily strength, vigor, or robustness; feeble, either constitutionally or from age, disease, etc.; infirm; of the organs of the body, deficient in functional energy, activity, or the like: as, a ''weak'' stomach; ''weak'' eyes.
{{smaller block|<poem>Min wlite [face] is wan,
& min herte ''woc'',
Mine dagis arren nei done.</poem>
{{right|''Rel. Antiq.'', I. 186.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I have, God woot, a large feeld to ere;
And ''wayke'' been the oxen in my plough.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 29.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A poor, infirm, ''weak'', and despised old man.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iii. 2. 20.}}}}

(''c'') Lacking moral strength or firmness; liable to waver or succumb when urged or tempted; deficient in steady principle or in force of character.
{{smaller block|Him that is ''weak'' in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations. {{right|Rom. xiv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Superior and unmoved; here only ''weak''
Against the charm of beauty’s powerful glance.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., viii. 532.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>If ''weak'' Women went astray,
Their Stars were more in Fault than they.</poem>
{{right|''Prior'', Hans Carvel.}}}}

(''d'') Lacking mental power, ability, or balance; simple; silly; foolish.
{{smaller block|It is privately whispered That King Henry was of a ''weak'' Capacity, and easily abused.
{{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 190.}}}}
{{smaller block|The tradition is that the water was conveyed from this pillar to the top of the famous temple, on which the people are so ''weak'' as to imagine there was a garden.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. i. 107.}}}}

(''e'') Unequal to a particular need or emergency; ineffectual or inefficacious; inadequate or unsatisfactory; incapable; impotent.

<poem>My ancient incantations are too ''weak.''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., v. 3. 27.}}}}

<poem>How vain is Reason, Eloquence how ''weak!''
If Pope must tell what Harcourt cannot speak.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Pope'', On the Hon. S. Harcourt.}}}}

<poem>One equal temper of heroic hearts,
Made ''weak'' by time and fate, but strong in will
To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', Ulysses.}}}}

(''f'') Incapable of support; not to be sustained or maintained; unsupported by truth, reason, or justice: as, a ''weak'' claim, assertion, argument, etc.

{{smaller block|A case so ''weak'' and feeble hath been much persisted in.
{{right|''Hooker.''}}}}

<poem>I know not what to say; my title ’s ''weak''—
Tell me, may not a king adopt an heir?</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., i. 1. 134.}}}}

(''g'') Deficient in force of utterance or sound; having little volume, loudness, or sonorousness; low; feeble; small.

{{smaller block|A voice, not softe, ''weake'', piping, womannishe.
{{right|''Ascham'', The Scholemaster, p. 39.}}}}

(''h'') Not abundantly or sufficiently impregnated with the essential, required, or usual ingredients, or with stimulating or nourishing substances or properties; not of the usual strength: as, ''weak'' tea; ''weak'' broth; a ''weak'' infusion; ''weak'' punch.

<poem>Sip this ''weak'' wine
From the thin green glass flask.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Browning'', Englishman in Italy.}}}}

(''i'') Deficient in pith, pregnancy, or point; lacking in vigor of expression: as, a ''weak'' sentence; a ''weak'' style.

<poem>There are to whom my satire seems too bold: . . .
The lines are ''weak'', another ’s pleased to say.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Pope'', Imit. of Hor., II. i. 5.}}}}

(''j'') Resulting from or indicating lack of judgment, discernment, or firmness; arising from want of moral courage, of self-denial, or of determination; injudicious: as, a ''weak'' compliance; a ''weak'' surrender. {{smaller block|<poem>If evil thence ensue,
She first his ''weak'' indulgence will accuse.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ix. 1186}}}}
{{smaller|(''k'') Slight; inconsiderable; trifling. [Rare.]}}
{{smaller block|Mine own ''weak'' merits.
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iii. 3. 187.}}}}
{{smaller|(''l'') In ''gram.'', inflected—(1) as a verb, by regular syllabic addition instead of by change of the radical vowel; (2) as a noun or an adjective, with less full or original differences of case- and number-forms: opposed to ''strong'' (which see). (''m'') Poorly supplied; deficient: as, a hand ''weak'' in trumps. (''n'') Tending downward in price: as, a ''weak'' market; corn was ''weak''.—'''The weaker sex.''' See ''sex''<sup>1</sup>.—'''The weaker vessel.''' See ''vessel''.—'''Weak accent, beat, or pulse,''' in ''music'', a comparatively unemphatic rhythmical unit: opposed to a ''heavy'' or ''strong accent'', etc. See ''rhythm''.—'''Weak election.''' See ''election''.—'''Weak side, weak point,''' that side, aspect, or feature of a person’s character or disposition in which he is most easily influenced or affected.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Guard thy heart
On this ''weak side'' where most our nature fails.</poem>
{{right|''Addison'', Cato, i. 1.}}}}
'''Weak verb.''' {{smaller|See def. 2 (''l'').}}

'''weak†''' (wēk), ''v.''   [< ME. ''weyken'', ''wayken'', ''woken'', ''wokien'', ''wakien'', < AS. ''wācian'', become weak, languish, vacillate (= MD. ''weecken'', become soft, D. ''weeken'', soak, = OHG. ''weichan'', MHG. G. ''weichen'', become weak), ''wǣcan'', make weak, weaken, soften, afflict, < ''wāc'', weak: see ''weak'', ''a.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To make weak; weaken.
{{smaller block|It is hey tyme; he drawyt fast home ward, and is ryte lowe browt, and sore ''weykid'' and feblyd.
{{right|''Paston Letters'', I. 444.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>We must toyle to make our doctrine good,
Which will empair the flesh and ''weak'' the knee.</poem>
{{right|''Dr. H. More'', Psychozoia, ii. 80.}}}}
'''2.''' To soften.
<poem>Ac grace groweth nat til goode wil gynne reyne,
And ''wokie'' thorwe good werkes wikkede hertes.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xv. 25.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become weak.   ''Chaucer.''

'''weak-built''' (wēk′bilt), ''a.'' Ill-founded. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Yet ever to obtain his will resolving,
Though ''weak-built'' hopes persuade him to abstaining.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 130.}}}}

'''weaken''' (wē′kn), ''v.''   [< ''weak'' + ''-en''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To become weak or weaker: as, he ''weakens'' from day to day.
{{smaller block|<poem>Somewhat to ''woken'' [var. ''wayken''] gan the peyne
By lengthe of pleynte. ''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 1144.</poem>
<poem>His notion ''weakens'', his discernings
Are lethargied. ''Shak.'', Lear, i. 4. 248.</poem>}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To make weak or weaker; lessen or reduce the strength, power, ability, influence, or quality of: as, to ''weaken'' the body or the mind; to ''weaken'' a solution or infusion by dilution; to ''weaken'' the force of an argument.
{{smaller block|So strong a Corrosive is Grief of Mind, when it meets with a Body ''weakened'' before with Sickness.
{{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 60.}}}}
{{smaller block|In all these things hath the Kingdome bin of late sore ''weak’nd.'' ''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., ii.
<poem>A languor came
Upon him, gentle sickness, gradually
''Weakening'' the man, till he could do no more.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Enoch Arden.}}}}

'''weakener''' (wēk′nėr), ''n.'' One who or that which weakens.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
